analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks on private gun sales, limits handgun purchases, and funds red-flag order laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by two Virginia Democratic senators, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nearly all private gun sales to go through a licensed dealer so a background check is run, capped unlicensed buyers at one handgun every 30 days, and required gun owners to report lost or stolen guns to police within 48 hours. It would have made it a federal crime to recklessly leave a loaded, unsecured gun where a child under 14 could reach it, barred people convicted of misdemeanor stalking and people under certain protective orders from having guns, and set up federal grants to help states and tribes run extreme risk protection order ("red flag") programs. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence: buyers and sellers in private sales who currently face no background check, communities affected by firearms trafficking through bulk handgun purchases, domestic violence victims whose abusers are dating partners rather than spouses, and people at risk of self-harm who could be separated from firearms through a court-ordered process with notice and a hearing. Law enforcement agencies would also receive grant funding and training support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence and domestic abuse

how_it_helps.text: Private firearms transfers between unlicensed individuals would have to go through a licensed dealer first, closing the exception that lets most private sales proceed with no background check [S2][S3].

An unlicensed person could buy no more than one handgun in a 30-day period, aimed at trafficking pipelines, with exemptions for law enforcement, licensed security companies, and people who pass an enhanced background check [S2][S3].

People convicted of misdemeanor stalking and people subject to qualifying protective orders would be barred from possessing firearms, extending restrictions that previously covered only felony convictions and spouse/cohabitant abusers to dating partners and stalkers [S2][S3].

The bill would establish a grant program to help states and Indian tribes implement extreme risk protection order laws, with at least 25 percent of grant funds going to law enforcement training, and gives those states preference in other Justice Department grants [S2][S3].

Gun owners would have to report lost or stolen firearms to law enforcement within 48 hours, and recklessly leaving a loaded, unsecured firearm where it endangers a child under 14 would become a federal offense [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms dealers would handle every private transfer and charge a fee for it (the bill bars any cap on that fee), private sellers and buyers would pay those fees and wait for checks, gun owners face a civil penalty of up to $250 for failing to report a lost or stolen gun and up to a year in jail and a $2,500 fine for recklessly leaving a loaded gun accessible to a young child, and taxpayers would fund the grant program. Gun sellers would also lose some bulk sales and sales to people who fail the expanded checks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, sellers, owners, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Red flag orders can be issued temporarily without the respondent present (an ex parte order lasting up to 30 days), which critics argue risks depriving people of their firearms before a full hearing; the bill addresses this with notice, a hearing within 30 days, and a due-process requirement, but courts would still make quick judgments on dangerousness [S3].

Routing all private transfers through licensed dealers adds cost, paperwork, and delay to ordinary transactions between family friends, neighbors, and hunting partners, though the bill exempts gifts and loans between close relatives, emergency loans, and supervised or range use [S3].

The one-handgun-per-30-days rule and the 48-hour lost/stolen reporting penalty fall on law-abiding owners and collectors, not just traffickers, and violations of the child-access rule carry criminal penalties up to one year in jail [S3].

The bill's grant program is authorized at 'such sums as are necessary' with no specific funding level, so states could be pushed to adopt red flag laws as a condition of federal grant preference without guaranteed federal money to run them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits are broad but diffuse: universal background checks, stalking and dating-partner prohibitions, and red flag laws are aimed at patterns of gun deaths (domestic violence, suicide, trafficking) that touch many households. The costs are real but narrow and mostly administrative — dealer fees on private transfers, penalties on careless owners, and due-process friction in red flag proceedings. The bill's drafters built in significant accommodations (family and emergency-transfer exemptions, enhanced-check exemptions from the handgun limit, due-process and return-of-firearms procedures), so the main honest objection is about burden on ordinary gun owners rather than design failure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on April 15, 2021, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the bill on April 15, 2021, with Sen. Mark Warner as cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 117th Congress [S5].
The only cosponsor listed for the entire two-year Congress was Sen. Warner; no Republican senators signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of expanded federal gun regulation, and firearms sellers and owners who would have faced new transfer, purchase, and reporting requirements, are better off because the bill never advanced; private-sale transactions continue without background checks.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of expanded gun regulation and gun sellers

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators supported the bill — Kaine and Warner — and no Republican cosponsored it; it never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown the full party split.

industries.note: The bill would force every private sale through a licensed dealer, generating paid facilitation work whose fees the bill explicitly bars capping, but it would also cut off unlicensed bulk handgun purchases and sales to people who fail checks. The gun retail industry generally opposed expanding background check requirements.

Fewer bulk purchases and a smaller pool of eligible buyers would reduce some sales volume, while red flag storage contracts and dealer-facilitated transfers would route new business through the licensed trade. Manufacturers as an industry lobby consistently opposed new federal gun restrictions.

The bill authorizes grants for personnel, training, protocols, and public awareness to run extreme risk protection order programs, with at least a quarter of funds reserved for law enforcement training.
